explanation: In C++, directly initializing class members can lead to several issues, such as requiring public access to members, placing the initialization burden on the user, and making the code fragile to changes in the class structure. A best practice is to use constructors to encapsulate initialization logic. This ensures that objects are initialized consistently, members can remain private for better encapsulation, and the class author handles the details. In real-world scenarios, this promotes maintainable code, reduces errors like forgotten initializers, and aligns with idiomatic C++ by following the Rule of Zero/Three/Five for resource management. Common pitfalls include exposing internal state (e.g., making members public) and manual initialization errors; these are avoided by centralizing initialization in constructors.
keywords: C++ constructor initialization, Initialize private members, Class member initialization
